title: Scene brief
description:
How to RUN one scene, for the GM, live — as distinct from what the scene IS, which is the episode's own scene entry. One file per scene in data/scene-briefs/, named <episodeId>--<sceneId>.json, read by the scene-runner panel (module/blank-inheritance/scripts/foundry/scene-runner.mjs) and rendered as a printed script.

The brief exists because the GM improvises the dialogue. It does not script a conversation; it gives the GM what they need to invent one in character — what each person wants, what they will and will not talk about, and how they sound — plus a checklist of what must actually happen, so nothing load-bearing gets lost in an hour of good talk.

NOT A SECURITY BOUNDARY. This file is fetched over plain HTTP by the module and the panel is GM-only by construction, but any logged-in client could request the URL. That is a deliberate, accepted trade (2026-09-09: "We don't need to firewall information from players"). Anything that genuinely must not reach a client belongs in a GM-only JournalEntry with ownership.default NONE, the way foundry/social-store.mjs and foundry/campaign-state.mjs both do it.

episodeRef.description: id of the episode.schema.json instance this scene belongs to.

sceneRef.description: The `id` of the scene inside that episode's `scenes` array — not its `order`, which moves when a scene is inserted.

title.description: What the GM sees at the top of the panel. Usually the scene's own title.

summary.description: One or two lines: what this scene is for. The thing to re-read thirty seconds before running it.

goal.description: What you want out of this scene, stated as an outcome you could check afterwards — "every player has spoken in character and every character has been told privately their screen flagged". Not a theme, not a mood. The thing that has to be true when it ends.

howToPlay.description: The register, in plain terms a GM can act on: pace, warmth, whether anyone is in danger. "A school medical crossed with a passport office. Warm, slow, faintly ridiculous. Nobody is in danger here."

runsAbout.description: Rough table time, e.g. "25 minutes". Scenes are short on purpose — a three-hour session is many small scenes, not three long ones.

mode.description: Which SF2E shape this scene resolves in. The strategy layer decides which scenes happen and what is at stake; SF2E decides how they resolve (design/strategy-layer.md). `exploration` means the real exploration rules, with attrition and resting.

spectrum.description: Where this scene sits between story and downtime (canon/decisions/D050.md): story = plot beats run as written; mixed = a story frame with events drawn from its deck; downtime = relaxed and low stakes, role-play, rest and events from the deck. The Scene Runner shows it as a coloured banner. Absent means story.

rest.description: This scene is a night's rest (D050). The Scene Runner offers one press to heal the characters of the players who came here.

hp.description: How much of each character's maximum HP the rest restores. Only the hospital restores all of it.

buff.description: What else the rest gives, in the words the GM reads: an automatic buff, or what a roll can earn.

events.description: The scene's event deck (D050): things that could happen, drawn at random in the Scene Runner. A drawn event the table witnessed never comes up again; one nobody saw goes back into the deck.

text.description: What happens, as the GM would run it.

check.description: The roll it offers, if any, e.g. "Society DC 15 to follow the argument".

note.description: GM-only: what it plants or pays off, and what it must not give away.

kind.description: What sort of event (D051). roll: a skill roll that produces a result. buff: something good happens to them. roleplay: a prompt to narrate in character. dilemma: a choice with a cost either way. informant: someone met by chance shares an unconsidered line of information. plot: more than it seems; the Runner alerts the GM and the scene falls back to ordinary running. danger: violence can happen; the players are never warned. Absent means roleplay.

prompt.description: What to ask the player or players, word for word, when the event asks them to narrate or decide.

outcomes.description: What each degree of success on the check gives.

episodes.description: The episodes this event can come up in. Absent means any.

shifts.description: What this event does to how the regulars feel about the group (D051): one-press buttons on the drawn event.

fight.description: D052: a "danger" event's theatre-of-the-mind shape. The players decide press or retreat; nothing here is rolled automatically, the GM narrates it.

foe.description: Who or what it is, in a phrase.

press.description: What happens if the characters press the attack: they need to get the foe down, and how the scene changes once that happens.

retreat.description: How it runs if they run instead.

surrender.description: When and how this foe gives up rather than die, if it does.

deckRef.description: Draw from a deck shared with other scenes (by that deck's id) instead of this brief's own, so what was witnessed in one scene is gone from the others.

accomplishment.description: Accomplishment XP, if this scene has an award attached. GM Core's own values: minor 10, moderate 30, major 80.

forWhat.description: What they have to actually do to earn it.

intro.description: How to get into the scene. The joins between scenes are where a session runs rough, so they are authored rather than improvised (design/strategy-layer.md §6).

where.description: Where they are and how they got here.

firstThing.description: The first thing they see or hear. The concrete detail you open on.

readAloud.description: Optional boxed text for the opening.

carriesIn.description: What a PREVIOUS scene's outcome changes about this one. The most-missed field in scene writing: a scene that reads identically whatever happened before it is not connected to anything.

when.description: The prior outcome, in plain terms — "if they took a prisoner in the lab".

then.description: What is different here because of it.

landmark.description: One named fixture in the room that everyone can state their position against — theatre of the mind fails silently without this, because a position relative to nothing is not a position. One sentence, one object: "the workbench," "the clock on the north wall."

holdInReserve.description: The detail you are NOT leading with — held back for the moment a player leans in and asks what they notice. Spending everything on the opening leaves nothing for that moment, and that moment is the one the technique exists to produce.

triggers.description: Same shape and purpose as a beat's own triggers[] (design/scene-triggers-and-depth.md §2) — matched against a <trig id="..."/> token in THIS intro's own readAloud, scoped as beatId "intro" for logging. A scene's opening narration is often the very first place an NPC is glimpsed (Shucks in intake-medicals' own intro, for one), so it needs the same inline capability a beat gets.

announce.description: reveal-name only. true also drops the banner ("the attendant is Kazue Tsurumi") when the name is told; false or absent just stamps the plate. There is no Shift key on an inline chip, so this is how a scene asks for the louder version.

position.description:
WHERE THE PARTY PHYSICALLY IS at this edge of the scene -- a coordinate anchor first, a togetherness state second. Ingram, 2026-09-22: "I want to literally have a set of coordinates for the players to move between and that needs to happen between EVERY scene change."

`locationRef` is that coordinate: a data/locations/ id, whose `derived.centroidPx` is a real point on the 12400x12400 campaign sheet at 1px = 1m. The pair (this scene's outro position, the next scene's intro position) IS the travel leg the Scene Runner animates -- core/travel-trigger.mjs's `needsTravel` fires when the two differ, and foundry/travel.mjs then plans a real route across the road graph. **A null locationRef means no map cut happens at that seam**, which is a hard cut the GM has to cover, so it is a real fault rather than a missing annotation -- the single exception being `scattered`, below.

locationRef.description: data/locations/ id. Null ONLY for `scattered`, which means deliberately off-map: the party is not anywhere the campaign map can show yet. Every other state owes a real location, because without one the automatic cut to the world map cannot fire.

state.description: scattered: off-map, positions not tracked -- reserved for the campaign's own opening, before anybody has arrived anywhere. individual: each PC at a different real place. converging: travelling toward one place, not yet arrived. together: all at the one locationRef, one GM track, one token to move. split: deliberately in two or more known groups, which the scene must say how to run -- and which means more than one thing moves on the map.

note.description: One or two sentences: where they actually are, and anything a GM needs to place a PC who was absent from the previous scene. For `split`, say which groups and who decides.

groups.description: Where each PART of the party is, when `state` is `split`. Added 2026-09-22 after Ingram: "That's great when the party is together, not great when the party splits up." Without this a split edge could say THAT the party had divided but not WHERE each half was, so the map could only ever move one marker. core/travel-trigger.mjs's travelLegsFor() turns these into one journey per group and foundry/travel.mjs animates them concurrently -- two groups crossing the city at the same time, which is what actually happened.

id.description: Stable within the scene, and matched by id across the two edges so a group that travels keeps one marker. Keep it plain: `tram-party`, `the-two-left-behind`.

label.description: What the marker is called on the map. Shown to the table, so write it as a GM would say it.

locationRef.description: data/locations/ id: where THIS group is. Null only if they are off-map, which for a group is almost always an error.

who.description: Who is in it, in plain words. The PCs do not exist yet, so this is a description of the split rather than a roster -- 'whoever went with the docket'.

outro.description: How to get out, and the scene's only hook back up to the strategy layer. This is where a scene stops being a scene and becomes a move on the board.

endsWhen.description: What actually ends it. Say it plainly so the scene does not sag past its own finish.

artefactRefs.description: ids from this brief's `artefacts` that the party can leave holding.

tracks.description: Which strategy-layer tracks this scene can move, and why. Suggestions for the GM, never automatic — the outcome belongs to play.

delta.description: Signed. null when the size depends on what happened.

why.description: What the party has to do for this to move.

onwards.description: What lands on tomorrow's board because of this scene.

transition.description: The connective tissue to the NEXT scene — not what happens there (that's `onwards`), the concrete, sayable, in-fiction reason the party actually goes. Added 2026-09-19 after a real gap: Kit Issue's own `onwards` said 'straight into the canteen' with nothing motivating it, and — found while fixing that — pointed at the wrong scene entirely (The Errand had since been inserted between them and already carried the correct line). A scene missing this is a scene whose next cut will read as arbitrary to the table, whatever `onwards` says happens there.

mechanism.description: ordered = a specific person tells them to go, no ambiguity, zero scatter risk (Canteen's tannoy). scheduled = the institution's own timetable moves them on with nobody having to say so (an induction day's fixed blocks). invited = a specific person or expectation is waiting for them, pulling rather than pushing. needed = a stated want (hunger, rest) that could genuinely fragment the party if the table takes it that way — use this deliberately, not by default, since Session 0/1's own scenes mostly need the six of them arriving together.

line.description: The actual sayable line or beat that delivers it — an order, an announcement, an institution's own momentum. What the GM says or does, not a description of it.

scatterRisk.description: True if this mechanism could plausibly split the party before the next scene needs them together. Nothing here should ever be a surprise to the GM mid-scene — this is decided at authoring time, not discovered live.

departure.description: WHERE THE PARTY GOES NEXT, and who decides (design/world-map-destinations.md). Absent means sent to the next scene in the episode's order, exactly as before this existed. Ingram, 2026-09-28: "sometimes players will get to choose where to go next and sometimes they won't be given a choice, sometimes players will be allowed to split off from the main group and sometimes the players will be forced to recombine into a group." Played on The City: players pick by clicking markers, the GM presses Go, each character's pawn walks, and the groups become a queue the Scene Runner runs one at a time.

kind.description: sent: the story decides, one destination. together: the players pick one destination as a group. free: each player picks; the same pick is the same group, so the party may split. muster: everyone to one place. arrive: each player picks how they come into the city, their pawn starts there, then `then` gathers them.

question.description: Put to the players across the top of The City. Plain words.

placeRef.description: For sent or muster written without destinations: the one place.

briefRef.description: For sent or muster written without destinations: the one scene.

label.description: For sent or muster written without destinations: what the one marker says.

id.description: Stable within this departure. Beats name it in forDestination.

label.description: Said to the players, on the marker and its card. Plain words.

blurb.description: One or two lines on the card: what is there and what it gives. Player-facing.

placeRef.description: data/locations/ id: where the marker stands, and where the pawn walks. For an arrive departure, where the player comes in from.

briefRef.description: The scene brief this destination leads to. Several destinations may share one (a rotation scene like The Long Afternoon).

image.description: A picture for the card. Normally left out: the thumbnail comes from the scene set's own art for this place, or for the scene it leads to (core/departures.mjs#thumbnailFor).

mystery.description: Blur and grey the thumbnail: the players know there is somewhere to go, not what it looks like.

mustGo.description: Law 21: mandatory, unmistakable on the map, and it takes everyone it is open to whatever they picked.

costsSlice.description: Law 20: shown on the marker. Decided separately from mustGo.

roomFor.description: How many can pick it. A full destination stays on the map, marked full.

pickedIn.description: Only players whose pick in the previous departure was one of these destination ids may take this one ('whoever went out has to get back in').

private.description: Seen only by the players it is open to, and the GM. A private pick never reaches the shared record.

needs.description: A condition said on the card, not enforced: 'a signed pass'.

mode.description: Arrive departures only: how they come in. Picks the card's emblem.

then.description: What follows once every group has been run: usually a muster that brings them back together.

writeDown.description: SHORT-HORIZON consequences: what the GM records tonight, in the session log and the tone ledger, before the table goes home. Split by horizon 2026-09-22 (design/scene-signoff.md's consequence radar) -- see carryForward for the medium horizon and nodeRefs for the long one.

triggers.description: Same shape as intro.triggers above, matched against this outro's own readAloud, scoped as beatId "outro" for logging.

announce.description: reveal-name only. true also drops the banner ("the attendant is Kazue Tsurumi") when the name is told; false or absent just stamps the plate. There is no Shift key on an inline chip, so this is how a scene asks for the louder version.

position.description: WHERE THE PARTY IS WHEN THIS SCENE CLOSES -- the FROM end of the travel leg into the next scene. The next scene's `intro.position.locationRef` is the TO end, and the pair is what the Scene Runner cuts to the world map to animate. If this is null, or equals the next scene's, no map cut fires and the table gets a hard cut instead of a journey.

note.description: One or two sentences: where they actually are, and anything a GM needs to place a PC who was absent from the previous scene. For `split`, say which groups and who decides.

groups.description: Where each PART of the party is, when `state` is `split`. Added 2026-09-22 after Ingram: "That's great when the party is together, not great when the party splits up." Without this a split edge could say THAT the party had divided but not WHERE each half was, so the map could only ever move one marker. core/travel-trigger.mjs's travelLegsFor() turns these into one journey per group and foundry/travel.mjs animates them concurrently -- two groups crossing the city at the same time, which is what actually happened.

label.description: What the marker is called on the map. Shown to the table, so write it as a GM would say it.

locationRef.description: data/locations/ id: where THIS group is. Null only if they are off-map, which for a group is almost always an error.

who.description: Who is in it, in plain words. The PCs do not exist yet, so this is a description of the split rather than a roster -- 'whoever went with the docket'.

artefacts.description:
Things the party can leave this scene permanently owning. An artefact becomes a real Foundry journal page whose ownership flips from GM-only to player-readable at the moment it is earned, and stays theirs for the rest of the campaign, browsable on the phone.

Distinct from `handouts`, which are shown transiently and revert when closed. An artefact is EARNED and KEPT — a fact about the Directorate the party took rather than were told, which reads differently at the table.

documentRef.description: Groups a redaction chain: several artefacts sharing a documentRef are the same document at different clearance levels (ideas/entries/redacted-document-chain.json, accepted). A Clearance rung therefore unlocks less-redacted versions of documents the party already holds.

clearance.description: Which Clearance rung this version corresponds to. 0 is the public version.

body.description: The artefact itself as HTML. Materialised into a journal page on first grant; editing this and re-pushing updates it in place.

imagePath.description: For an artefact that is a photograph or a scan rather than text.

earnedBy.description: GM-facing: what the party has to do to end up holding this.

gmNote.description: What the GM should know that the players should not.

clockRef.description: id of a subsystem.schema.json instance whose pools this scene runs on a visible clock — e.g. a shift's twelve walls as a diminishing pool, spent down by that subsystem's `spends`. null for the many scenes with no clock.

cast.description: Everyone the GM might have to be, in this scene. Includes walk-ons who will never have a file in data/npcs/ — a brief for three lines of foreman is still worth thirty seconds of authoring.

npcRef.description: id of a data/npcs/*.json file, when this is a real recurring NPC. The NPC file wins on identity — do NOT restate a name here for someone whose real name is still an open naming placeholder.

label.description: Display name for a walk-on with no NPC file ("Sergeant Ihara", "A man with a dog"). Ignored when npcRef resolves to a named NPC.

role.description: One line of who they are to this scene — "works foreman", "the Directorate's information officer".

called.description: What the TABLE calls this person until they learn the real name: "the attendant", "the man in the grey coat". Present means their name is held back (core/stage-names.mjs): the stage plate, arrival banner and splash show this line until the name is told, and their stage id and portrait file name stay anonymous. Absent means shown by name as always. The real name is label (or the NPC file). Keep it a description, never a name or a hint at one.

nameOnArrival.description: Only meaningful with called. true means this person is introduced by name the moment they arrive (a name badge, a teacher at the front of the class), so the table is told their name as they are staged. Without it the name waits for a Name key press or a reveal-name trigger.

arrival.description: How they come into the scene, reusing the built sting tiers (core/sting.mjs). splash is the full-screen introduction and is NPC-only — see core/splash.mjs. null means they are simply already there.

walkOn.description: True for someone deliberately disposable — the panel renders them small and does not offer to stage a portrait. "Give him three lines and never bring him back."

brief.description: The improvisation aid. Everything here is GM-only and permanently so — unlike npc.schema.json's socialProfile.facts, which are player-facing knowledge revealed through play. The two are complements: facts are what the table can learn, this is how you play the person.

wants.description: What they are trying to ACHIEVE in this conversation. The single most useful field — it decides what they do when the players surprise you.

opensWith.description: What they raise first if left to themselves. Their agenda, not yours.

willDiscuss.description: Topics they will engage with, and what they give up on each.

note.description: What they actually say or concede here.

willNotDiscuss.description: Hard lines. What they deflect, refuse, or lie about — and why, because the why is what lets you improvise the refusal in their voice instead of just saying no.

coercible.description: What could be got out of them under pressure, and what it takes. Distinct from willDiscuss: this is what they give up only when leaned on.

how.description: What kind of pressure works — leverage, sympathy, authority, a named Fact.

challengeRef.description: id of a challenge.schema.json instance if getting it is an actual roll.

voice.description: How they sound. The panel sets `samples` in a different face from everything around it, because a line you might actually say out loud is not the same kind of text as a note about them.

register.description: The one-line characterisation — "clipped, dry, never raises his voice".

tics.description: Verbal habits worth reaching for — a repeated phrase, a way of pausing, what they call people.

samples.description: Real lines, in their voice. Not a script to read — a tuning fork. Three good ones beat twenty.

attitude.description: SF2E attitude toward the party on a first meeting.

questions.description: Questions the group are likely to ask, answered in their voice.

statblock.description: Until the NPC generator exists: the proposed level and archetype, for making the stat block with Ingram.

byAttitude.description: How they behave toward the group at each attitude (D051). The Scene Runner shows the line for their attitude now, so the scene reads differently as the group rises or falls in their eyes.

faction.description: D052: a kebab-case id of the group this regular really belongs to, shared by every regular who is the same group wherever they appear (e.g. two haunts' dock workers both writing "the-dock-crews"). Shifting one member's attitude shifts the whole faction's, kept globally rather than per place -- fall out with one gang member and the whole gang hates the group. A regular's attitude as played is the worse of their own and their faction's. Omit when there is no real group.

doors.description: D052: this regular's own decision tree of what their attitude opens and closes -- the promise that a worse attitude makes the group's lives harder next time, made concrete and playable rather than left as a number.

kind.description: opens = available while at this attitude or better. closes = shut while at this attitude or worse.

text.description: The concrete, playable consequence -- a better seat, a tab, backstage access; or a refusal, a raised DC, a report to the office.

beats.description: What has to happen, in the order it probably happens. The GM ticks these off live. Order here is authoring order, not enforcement — `after` and `when` carry real sequencing where it matters.

id.description: Stable — tick state is keyed on it, so renaming a beat mid-campaign forgets whether it happened.

kind.description: action = something happens in the fiction. check = resolved by a roll (needs challengeRef). reveal = puts something in front of the players (needs handoutRef). combat = a real encounter runs (needs encounterRef; subsystemRef if a hazard/clock runs alongside it). Defaults to action.

text.description: Stage direction — what this beat IS, in the GM's own shorthand. Rendered as prose.

readAloud.description: Verbatim boxed text, if there is any. Set apart typographically from `text`, because one is a note to yourself and the other is a thing you say to six people.

direction.description: How to PLAY it, as distinct from what happens — "this must land as nothing", "play it as an entrance". The note a director gives an actor.

mandatory.description: Whether the scene has failed at its job if this never happens. Deliberately independent of every other axis: a mandatory beat can be a passive check nobody is told about, and an optional beat can be the loudest thing in the scene (doctrine Law 20 — mandatory and slot-consuming are two different tests).

delivery.description:
Who receives it. table = everyone at once (the default). each = every player in turn, publicly -- the GM goes round the table and gives each character their own version of this beat, so six people get six distinct moments rather than one shared one. solo = one player, privately; the panel offers a targeted push rather than making the GM take somebody out of the room. passive = nobody is told anything happened, including that a check was made.

The value "each" exists because this campaign leans on that structure heavily and nothing could see it. A per-player go-round -- six bespoke questions in The Hammer, six crew chiefs in Familiarisation, six physical states in Zero Six Hundred -- is six moments of spotlight, and every structural measure counted it as one beat of narration and flagged the scene as low-agency. A structure no tool can see is a structure that eventually gets "fixed".

npcRef.description: The `id` of a cast entry above, when this beat belongs to one person — the panel surfaces their brief alongside it.

handoutRef.description: id of an entry in `handouts` below.

challengeRef.description: id of a challenge.schema.json instance in data/challenges/. Checks are NOT inlined here — challenge.schema.json already models a handful of DC'd checks with full four-degree outcomes, and episode.scenes[].challengeRefs was already wired for exactly this.

checkRef.description: The `id` of one check inside that challenge. A challenge is "one or a handful" of checks, so a scene's rolls group into one file per scene rather than one file per roll; this names which of them this beat is.

encounterRef.description: id of an encounter.schema.json instance in data/encounters/, for a kind:"combat" beat.

subsystemRef.description: id of a subsystem.schema.json instance in data/subsystems/, when a hazard/clock/pool runs alongside this beat (a combat beat with an environmental hazard, or a pure subsystem scene with no encounter at all).

gmTool.description: Added 2026-09-19 (#176) — found live when a beat's own text said 'show every player the real catalogue' and there was no button anywhere to do that, only a macro UUID buried in the episode journal's description field. Set this when a beat's text implies a specific GM-side tool the panel can actually open in one click, rather than leaving it to prose plus a remembered macro. `id` must be a key the Scene Runner's own GM_TOOLS registry (foundry/scene-runner.mjs) recognises — this is deliberately NOT a free string, because a typo here should fail loudly (no button rendered) rather than silently.

id.description: e.g. "equipment-locker". Matched against the Scene Runner's GM_TOOLS registry, not invented per-beat.

label.description: Button text — "Open Equipment Locker", not the tool's internal id.

after.description: id of a beat this cannot happen before. Ordering only — it does not hide this beat.

nodeRefs.description: ids of Node entries (design/node-registry.md) this beat touches — a mystery-ledger plant, an open arc in a bible/dossier file's `## Arcs` section, an open-questions.json/naming-placeholders.json entry. State the fact here as a reference, not as restated prose; the canonical version lives at the Node.

when.description: Makes this beat conditional. This is how a scene branches: divergent paths are sibling beats with different `when` clauses off the same predecessor, rather than a nested tree — one shape, no renderer recursion, and it matches subsystem.complications' own triggerCondition idiom.

beatRef.description: The beat whose outcome gates this one.

degrees.description: Which degrees of success on beatRef's challenge open this path. Four degrees, never five — a plain Failure with no listed effect is what reads as 'neutral' in play. Omit to mean 'whenever beatRef happens at all'.

condition.description: Free prose for a GM-judged trigger with no mechanical test — "if a PC engages him afterward". The panel shows it as something the GM can open by hand.

forDestination.description: The departure destinations this beat belongs to (outro.departure of the scene the party left). The Scene Runner shows the beat with the names of the players there, and hides it when nobody went -- the structured form of a 'for players who chose X' condition (design/world-map-destinations.md §7).

choicePoint.description: Formalizes this beat as a real, disclosed fork for the table — added 2026-09-19 at Ingram's request: "You should probably clearly mark in the scene runner when I'm offering the group a chance to make a choice... leaving room for the group to decide to take a third option that is also possible and that we didn't think about." Distinct from `when` (branches on what already happened) — a choicePoint is presented TO the players as a live decision in the moment, and the panel should render it visibly as one, not as ordinary prose.

label.description: What the choice IS, stated plainly — "how do they file the requisition".
The option, stated plainly, in terms the GM can say out loud.

consequence.description: What it actually does — GM-facing; not necessarily told to the players before they choose.

allowsInventedOption.description: Should almost always be true. A third option the table invents on the spot is not a failure of prep — price or adjudicate it in the spirit of the authored options rather than refusing it.

note.description: Anything else worth having to hand — a payoff this plants, a callback it pays off.

facts.description: Canon facts this beat tells the table, by id (canon/world). The checker makes sure the players may know each one by this scene. See design/story-data-refactor.md.

gmFacts.description: Canon facts this beat relies on for the GM, by id. Never said to the table.

triggers.description: Added 2026-09-20 (design/scene-triggers-and-depth.md §2) — buttons a GM presses INLINE, mid-sentence, at the exact word in `text`/`readAloud` where an author placed a `<trig id="..."/>` token. Each entry here is one recognised id; a token in the prose with no matching entry renders as a visible `⚠ trig:unknown-id` error rather than silently doing nothing (core/inline-triggers.mjs). Every kind is a thin dispatch to a function that already exists elsewhere in the module (summonToStage, removeFromStage, the handout reveal, the GM_TOOLS registry, the sf2e check enricher) — nothing here recomputes anything, and every press calls the existing recordLogEntry with a timestamp, matching doctrine Law 12/15.

id.description: Scoped to this beat, like checkRef is scoped to a challengeRef — matched against a <trig id="..."/> token in this same beat's text or readAloud.

kind.description: npc-enter/npc-exit call the existing stage functions with this cast member's id. reveal-name tells the table that cast member's real name (they need a `called` line, or there is nothing to tell). reveal-handout calls the existing handout reveal. gm-tool calls the existing GM_TOOLS registry by toolId — not a second registry. post-check posts the existing sf2e @Check enricher for checkRef. note writes a plain log line with no other side effect, for a moment worth marking with nothing mechanical attached.

npcRef.description: id of a `cast[]` entry above. Required for npc-enter/npc-exit/reveal-name.

announce.description: reveal-name only. true also drops the banner ("the attendant is Kazue Tsurumi") when the name is told; false or absent just stamps the plate. There is no Shift key on an inline chip, so this is how a scene asks for the louder version.

arrival.description: npc-enter only. Overrides this specific entrance's tier independent of the cast member's own default `arrival` — the same NPC can enter quietly once and be announced later, authored as two different triggers.

handoutRef.description: id of an entry in this brief's `handouts`. Required for reveal-handout.

toolId.description: Matched against the Scene Runner's existing GM_TOOLS registry — same id space as a beat's own top-level `gmTool.id`, just reachable from inline prose instead of only from the beat's action row.

checkRef.description: id of a check inside this beat's own `challengeRef`. Required for post-check.

label.description: Short GM-facing text — the button's tooltip and what the log entry says happened. "Taka arrives", not "npc-enter: taka".

solo.description: reveal-handout / note only. Mirrors an ordinary beat's own delivery:"solo" — pushed to one player privately rather than the whole table.

handouts.description: Documents and images this scene can put in front of players. Staged here so revealing one is a single deliberate click at the right moment; never automatic (doctrine Law 17 — confirm anything the players will see). Revealing one also FILES it (Ingram, 2026-09-26): it opens on their screens and stays in their Papers journal folder for the rest of the campaign, readable and never editable, so a reveal is never transient (module/blank-inheritance/scripts/core/handouts.mjs plans it, foundry/handouts.mjs carries it out).

title.description: What the GM sees in the panel.

journalRef.description: Repo id of an EXISTING journal this lives in, resolved to a Foundry document by the module's own deterministic-id derivation. Use this for a document that belongs to the world rather than to one scene.

pageName.description: Which page inside it. Page-level ownership is real in Foundry, so one page per clearance level is the supported way to hold several redactions of the same document (design/visual-identity.md §3b).

body.description: The document itself, authored inline, as HTML. The adapter creates or updates a journal page from it on demand, so a handout that exists only for this scene needs no separate file and no sync run to change. Paper documents use the classes in module/blank-inheritance/styles/bi-papers.css (`bi-paper`, a letterhead, stamps, a tear-off slip). Two campaign tags are rendered to plain HTML before anything reaches Foundry, whose sanitiser would otherwise strip them and publish their contents bare: the redaction pipeline's `<redact c="n">` (removed below the reader's clearance), and `<typed>…</typed>` for words struck on a typewriter, with `machine="…"` naming a typewriter whose fault it carries (core/handouts.mjs TYPEWRITERS) and the self-closing `<typed field="character" fallback="…"/>` for the reader's own character's name. An unprocessed tag is a hard error, never a silent leak. sf2e's inline `@Check[...]` survives into the pushed page.

personal.description: One private copy per player instead of one shared page: each player's copy has their own character's name typed into any `<typed field="character"/>` gap, and only they can read it. For a document every character received separately, like the acceptance letter. Default false.

imagePath.description: For a handout that is just a picture — pushed with Foundry's own image share rather than as a journal.

gmNotes.description: What the GM should know about this document that the players should not.

catchables.description: The things a careful reader can notice in it. Not hints to give out — the list to check against when a player says "wait, hang on", so you know immediately whether they have found something real.

challengeRef.description: The roll for engaging with the text properly, if there is one.

gmModifiers.description: Secret, GM-only adjustments to a roll that the player must never see — an instrument that works better in some places than others, a circumstance nobody has named yet. The panel shows the GM the adjusted DC and posts a blind check, so the player rolls against a number they are never told (core/roll-intent.mjs already carries the blind-roll path; we do not recompute anything sf2e computes).

label.description: GM-facing name for the thing being modified.

value.description: A flat modifier for this scene, when it does not vary.

byLocation.description: Keyed by a location/scene id where the modifier differs. The whole point of a varying hidden modifier is that the players build a false theory about when the thing works, so the variance must be authored across the campaign rather than improvised twice.

offers.description: Time-limited scheduling leads this scene puts on the board — the same shape as data/campaign/config.json's timeEconomy.options, plus the expiresOn that core/commitments.mjs already reads and no data file has ever set. "Leads decay differently" is exactly per-offer expiry.

expiresOn.description: A moment key ("d9:evening"). The offer survives THROUGH the quarter it names — "expires tonight" has to mean you can still do it tonight.

nodeRefs.description: ids of Node entries (design/node-registry.md) this scene touches as a whole, rather than one specific beat. LONG HORIZON: this is where a campaign-scale plant's status lives, and the only legitimate home for the question of which chapter pays it off. Naming a payoff chapter or a numbered Ledger entry in a beat's prose instead is the drift bug found live 2026-09-19 (design/node-registry.md §11 Bug A), and the Sign-Off's M23 now fails a scene that does it.

carryForward.description: MEDIUM-HORIZON consequences: what the next writing pass has to answer before the following episodes can be written. Rendered as part of the scene-close prompt. Split by horizon 2026-09-22 (design/scene-signoff.md, the consequence radar): this field and outro.writeDown previously carried word-for-word identical descriptions and were used 2 and 26 times respectively, which is the duplication-then-drift pattern design/data-ownership.md exists to stop. Short horizon is outro.writeDown; long horizon is a Node via nodeRefs.

reactionPrompts.description: Added 2026-09-19, REPURPOSED 2026-09-22. One sentence each, authored ahead of time rather than typed live: a likely outcome, a way the scene could go badly, or a specific NPC/moment worth checking the table's reaction to. These are now the AGENDA for the in-depth session review -- the questions someone asks about this scene afterwards. The Close Scene dialogue records them verbatim onto the session-log entry when the GM's verdict is Note or Panic, so the review opens with this scene's own specific questions instead of a blank page. They are no longer rated in-session: the dialogue used to render each as a row of 0-10 buttons, which on a five-prompt scene put fifty-five buttons between a GM and the accept button they could not reach -- see core/scene-close.mjs's header for the live failure and the rebuild. Distinct from `outro.writeDown`, which asks the GM to write free text at the table; this asks nothing of them during play at all. Complements `outro.writeDown` and does not replace it -- write prompts that are genuinely worth interrogating later, not a restatement of every beat.

text.description: The one-sentence outcome or moment to be examined in the review, phrased as something specific enough to ask a real question about.

scaleNote.description: Optional short caption that used to anchor the retired 0-10 button row, e.g. "0 = fell flat, 10 = table loved it". Kept because the existing ones read as useful context on what a good or bad outcome for this prompt would have been, which the review still wants; nothing renders it at the table any more, so there is no reason to write new ones.

temptations.description: Added 2026-09-20 (design/scene-triggers-and-depth.md §3). One sentence each, in the GM's own voice, ready to say out loud unprompted if the table stalls or nobody bites on the obvious hook. Not tied to any one beat — a GM reaches for one whenever the scene needs a nudge, not at a scripted moment. Never mandatory, never a check, the cheapest possible way to add width to a scene that's gone quiet.

text.description: The line itself, ready to say. "Nobu's clearly got more in the back than the docket says — worth asking?"

rumours.description: The rumour mill (D051): three sets per episode. A player names any skill they can justify and rolls blind. Critical failure: three lies. Failure: two lies and one truth. Success: two truths and one lie. Critical success: three truths. At most one rumour in a set touches the plot.

haunt.description: This scene is a haunt (D051): a place the group often comes back to, run as a menu rather than a script. Its regulars are its cast; its events are its deck.

everyVisit.description: What is always true here, read or described on every arrival.

changes.description: How the place can change over the campaign, as the city changes.

discovery.description: D052: offered through "somewhere new" rather than picked by name -- the players don't know what they'll get or where they'll go. Discovered places carry riskier and more powerful buffs, debuffs and encounters than the ordinary rests.

oneTime.description: D052: this discovery plays once, not as a repeatable haunt -- e.g. the first night's Magic Show.

upgrades.description: D052: how this repeat location gets better for the group with use. Unlocked by hand in the Scene Runner once the story earns it.

how.description: How the group earns it in play.

rest.description: If unlocking it changes the rest itself, the new values; otherwise the scene's own rest stands.

setbacks.description: D052: how a story event can make this location less effective, for a while or for good. Triggered by hand in the Scene Runner.

text.description: One short sentence, as the rumour is told.

plot.description: Touches the actual plot, to reveal or mislead. At most one per set.

hint.description: GM-only: what else this invites a guess at, or what it points to.

fact.description: GM-only: the canon fact a plot rumour reveals or misleads about.
